claim: Autologous iliac crest bone graft harvest has been associated with long-term donor site pain in up to 25% of patients.
source: Thus, autologous iliac crest bone graft (ICBG) remains the gold standard in both settings, but its harvest has been associated with long-term donor site pain in up to 25% of patients and its use in the posterolateral spine has a non-union rate nearing 40% (Noshchenko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noshchenko et al., 2014

claim: Autologous iliac crest bone graft use in the posterolateral spine has a non-union rate nearing 40%.
source: Thus, autologous iliac crest bone graft (ICBG) remains the gold standard in both settings, but its harvest has been associated with long-term donor site pain in up to 25% of patients and its use in the posterolateral spine has a non-union rate nearing 40% (Noshchenko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noshchenko et al., 2014

claim: Alternative bone graft options have not been clinically proven to be suitable as effective autograft substitutes.
source: A variety of alternative bone graft options are currently available (i.e. allograft, demineralized bone matrix); however, none have been clinically proven to be suitable as effective autograft substitutes (Boden, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boden, 2000

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway is central to the development and homeostasis of bone.
source: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway stands out as a promising pathway to target for bone regenerative therapies given that it is central to the development and homeostasis of bone and because it has complex crosstalk with canonical BMP signaling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Wnt signaling in bone biology

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway has complex crosstalk with canonical BMP signaling.
source: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway stands out as a promising pathway to target for bone regenerative therapies given that it is central to the development and homeostasis of bone and because it has complex crosstalk with canonical BMP signaling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pathway interactions

claim: Upon binding of Wnt ligands to the LRP5/6 receptor, β-catenin accumulates and translocates into the nucleus.
source: Upon the binding of Wnt ligands to the LRP5/6 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5/6) receptor, β-catenin accumulates and translocates into the nucleus where it forms complexes with TCF/Lef1 (T-cell factor/lymphoid enhancer factor) transcription factors (Baron and Rawadi, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baron and Rawadi, 2007

claim: β-catenin forms complexes with TCF/Lef1 transcription factors in the nucleus.
source: Upon the binding of Wnt ligands to the LRP5/6 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5/6) receptor, β-catenin accumulates and translocates into the nucleus where it forms complexes with TCF/Lef1 (T-cell factor/lymphoid enhancer factor) transcription factors (Baron and Rawadi, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baron and Rawadi, 2007

claim: The β-catenin/TCF/Lef1 complex initiates transcription of various osteogenic target genes.
source: This complex then initiates the transcription of various osteogenic target genes.
evidence: This follows from the established mechanism of Wnt signaling

claim: Osteogenic target genes enhance proliferation, expansion, and survival of osteoblasts, significantly increasing osteogenesis.
source: In osteoblasts, these genes enhance proliferation, expansion, and survival, significantly increasing osteogenesis (Boden et al., 1995; Nusse, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boden et al., 1995 and Nusse, 2005

claim: Sclerostin binds to the LRP5/6 receptor and disrupts the interaction between extracellular Wnts and their receptor.
source: The regulation of intracellular canonical Wnt signaling is ensured physiologically by the Wnt antagonist, sclerostin, which, upon binding the LRP5/6 receptor, disrupts the interaction between extracellular Wnts and their receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sclerostin's mechanism of action

claim: Sclerostin is a potent inhibitor of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
source: This potent inhibitor of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is secreted primarily by osteocytes and functions to inhibit bone formation (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: Sclerostin is secreted primarily by osteocytes.
source: This potent inhibitor of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is secreted primarily by osteocytes and functions to inhibit bone formation (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: Sclerostin functions to inhibit bone formation.
source: This potent inhibitor of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway is secreted primarily by osteocytes and functions to inhibit bone formation (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: Anti-sclerostin monoclonal antibodies have been shown to enhance bone healing in ovariectomized rats.
source: Anti-sclerostin mAbs have been shown to enhance bone healing in ovariectomized rats and bone mineral density in humans by increasing bone formation and mass due to enhanced osteoblast function (Suen et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2012; Recker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Suen et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2012; Recker et al., 2015

claim: Anti-sclerostin monoclonal antibodies have been shown to enhance bone mineral density in humans.
source: Anti-sclerostin mAbs have been shown to enhance bone healing in ovariectomized rats and bone mineral density in humans by increasing bone formation and mass due to enhanced osteoblast function (Suen et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2012; Recker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Suen et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2012; Recker et al., 2015

claim: The loop 2 region of sclerostin is the known binding site for functional anti-sclerostin antibodies.

claim: Mutations in the Leu-90 to Asn-103 residues of the loop 2 region resulted in the inability for sclerostin to bind to LRP5/6.
source: Mutational analyses have shown that mutations in the Leu-90 to Asn-103 residues of the loop 2 region resulted in the inability for sclerostin to bind to LRP5/6 (Boschert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boschert et al., 2016

claim: A mutation of single amino acids in the loop 2 region (Asp-92 or Ile-94) affects the binding of sclerostin to LRP6.
source: Similarly, a mutation of single amino acids in the loop 2 region (Asp-92 or Ile-94) is known to affect the binding of sclerostin to LRP6 (Boschert et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boschert et al., 2013

claim: A murine sclerostin mutant with Cys-84 and Cys-142 exchange has reduced binding affinity to LRP5/6.
source: Other studies, however, have shown that a murine sclerostin mutant with Cys-84 and Cys-142 exchange (resulting in the removal of the third disulfide bond of the cystine knot) has reduced binding affinity to LRP5/6 (Boschert et al., 2013), suggesting that elements outside the flexible loop 2 region are also important for proper sclerostin function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Boschert et al., 2013

claim: Three sclerostin small-molecule inhibitors (F1, VA1, and C07) were able to effectively enhance Wnt3a-induced reporter activity at suboptimal dose of Wnt3a.

claim: Treatment of transfected cells with sclerostin SMI compounds alone (without Wnt3a protein) did not show any significant induction of reporter activity.

claim: All three sclerostin SMIs competed with sclerostin to prevent labeled sclerostin from binding to LRP5.

claim: The SMI C07 prevented approximately 40% of sclerostin from binding to LRP5.

claim: All three sclerostin SMIs dose-dependently enhanced Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the presence of a suboptimal dose of 10 ng/ml of Wnt3a.

claim: The efficacy of the individual SMIs for enhancing Wnt signaling was C07>VA1>F1.
source: The efficacy of the individual SMIs were as follows: C07>VA1>F1.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental results from reporter assays

claim: All three sclerostin SMIs inhibited the accumulation of phosphorylated (inactive) β-catenin in murine MC3T3-E1 and MSC cells.

claim: All three sclerostin SMI candidates exhibited a significant potentiating effect on BMP-induced luciferase activity at all doses of BMP-2 tested (50, 100, and 200 ng/ml).

claim: The efficacy of individual SMIs for potentiating BMP signaling was C07>VA1>F1.
source: The efficacy of individual SMIs were as follows: C07>VA1>F1.

claim: All three sclerostin SMIs significantly increased the duration of pSmad1/5Cter compared to untreated controls.

claim: C07 resulted in the greatest increase in BMP signaling duration among the three SMIs.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, all three sclerostin SMIs significantly increased the duration of pSmad1/5Cter compared to untreated controls, with C07 resulting in the greatest increase in BMP signaling duration.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B with western blot time-course data

claim: The duration of the pSmad1/5Cter signal is controlled by canonical Wnt-mediated phosphorylation of GSK3b.
source: These results suggest that after phosphorylation by the BMP receptor, the duration of the pSmad1/5Cter signal is controlled by canonical Wnt-mediated phosphorylation GSK3b.

claim: The intensity of the Smad1/5/8 response is determined mostly by BMPs, but also canonical Wnt activation.

evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing pathway interactions

claim: The duration of the Smad1/5/8 response is at least partially controlled by Wnt/β-catenin signaling via GSK3b phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, out data suggests that the intensity of the Smad1/5/8 response is determined mostly by BMPs, but also canonical Wnt activation, while the duration of the Smad1/5/8 response is at least partially controlled by Wnt/β-catenin signaling via GSK3b phosphorylation.

claim: All three SMI candidates significantly increased the expression of Id1 (16.5×, 17×, 17.5× over baseline for F1, VA1, and C07, respectively).

claim: Recombinant murine sclerostin (80 ng/ml) completely reversed the osteoinductive effects of rhBMP-2 (20 ng/ml).

claim: BMP-2 treatment led to a >50% reduction in the OPG:RANKL ratio in MC3T3-E1 cells.

claim: VA1 at 500 mM as a standalone drug without ICBG achieved a 17% fusion rate.

claim: No significant differences in bone quality are seen between rabbits that received C07 alone and those that received C07 and autologous ICBG.
